title: [Chapitre] VIII. Analysis situs (quatrième mouture) : notes manuscrites (26/06-04/07/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (Analysis situs, 4th version, 1986). Grothendieck is building a purely combinatorial model of one-dimensional 'figures'. He starts from a totally ordered set L. The set M of elementary pieces consists of points P_a (a in L) and segments S_{a,b} (a<b). Each piece X has a 'trace' |X|.

Two symmetric 'foreignness' relations are used:
- X || Y means the closed traces are disjoint.
- X |o| Y is an 'open' version. Under it, P_a |o| S_{a,b}, since an endpoint does not meet the open segment. A piece is never |o| to itself.

For a subset Φ of M he defines cosupp°(Φ) as the set of pieces |o| to every element of Φ. He then sets supp°(Φ) = cosupp°(cosupp°(Φ)). Supp is the analogous double polar for ||. This is the classical polarity (Galois-connection) closure attached to a symmetric relation. 'Anti-influence' is the order-reversing property of the polar. It gives cosupp°(Φ) ∩ supp°(Φ) = ∅ by irreflexivity.

The page lists corollaries of Lemma 1 (previous page: supp(X) = Omb(X), the 'shadow', i.e. all pieces whose trace lies in |X|).
- Cor 1: Supp({P_a}) = {P_a}. The header says this also equals Supp°({P_a}).
- Cor 2: Supp({S_{a,b}}) consists of all P_x with a≤x≤b and all S_{x,y} with a≤x<y≤b. This is the closed shadow.
- Cor 3: Supp°({S_{a,b}}) = Supp({S_{a,b}}) minus ∂S_{a,b} = {P_a, P_b}. That is, all P_x with a<x<b and all S_{x,y} with a≤x<y≤b. This is the 'open shadow' Omb°(S_{a,b}). It still contains S_{a,b} itself and the sub-segments abutting the endpoints. Only the endpoint points are removed.
- Cor 4: Supp°({S_{a,b}, P_a}) = Omb°(S_{a,b}) ∪ {P_a}, and similarly with P_b. These are the half-open segments.

So the polar closure under the open relation automatically produces closed, open and half-open pieces. It is a combinatorial interior/closure calculus for tame one-dimensional figures.

Proof of Cor 1 (begun here, finished on the next page).
- If a is the least or greatest element, cosupp°(P_a) = M − {P_a}. Hence the closure is {P_a}.
- Otherwise pick x<a<y. Membership in the closure forces X |o| S_{x,a} and X |o| S_{a,y}. This pins the extent δX to a.
- This is where Hypothesis H from the previous page is used: if a is not minimal, some x<a exists.

The crossed-out first attempt (cosupp°(P_a) = L_{<a} ∪ L_{>a}, etc.) is the same argument, abandoned for the case split.
errors: Notational tension: the previous page's margin defines Omb°(X) as the pieces Y with |Y| strictly contained in |X|, which would exclude S_{a,b} itself. Cor 3 instead identifies Omb°(S_{a,b}) with an 'open shadow' that contains S_{a,b} and excludes only P_a and P_b. Grothendieck crossed out and re-inserted '= Omb°(S_ab)', showing he was adjusting the definition of Omb° on the fly.
Proof of Cor 1 is incomplete on this page (continued on p.93). Its case 'a is extremal' silently uses that every X ≠ P_a is |o| to P_a. That holds only for the open relation, not for ||.
Minor: the equality Supp(P_a) = Supp°(P_a) asserted in the header is stated without separate justification. It follows from the same case analysis.

ideas.what: Closure of sets of pieces via the double polar of a symmetric 'disjointness' relation (cosupp, supp = cosupp∘cosupp)
ideas.modern_name: Polarity / Galois connection closure; orthogonality-space closure (as in formal concept analysis or orthoclosure)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Birkhoff (polarities, 1940); Ore; Wille (formal concept analysis, 1982); orthogonality spaces (Foulis–Randall et al.)
ideas.where_published: Only in these unpublished Analysis situs notes, as far as known

ideas.what: Using an 'open' versus 'closed' disjointness relation so that polar closure yields closed, open and half-open segments (interior = closure minus boundary)
ideas.modern_name: Combinatorial point-free interior/closure on a finite cell/poset model of the line; cf. o-minimal cell decomposition and pointless topology
ideas.usually_credited_to: Pointless topology tradition (Whitehead/de Laguna mereotopology, region connection calculus); o-minimality (van den Dries, Pillay–Steinhorn)
ideas.where_published: Tame topology is only programmatically sketched in Esquisse d'un programme (1984); this axiomatics is unpublished

ideas.what: Order-theoretic hypotheses on L (existence of a lower element when a is not minimal; density) needed for the computations
ideas.modern_name: Linear order axioms (non-extremal elements have neighbours)

missed.claim: Grothendieck's 1986 approach to tame topology works mereotopologically: pieces plus a contact/foreignness relation, with closure given by the double polar. This is essentially the region-connection / mereotopology framework developed independently in AI and qualitative spatial reasoning (Clarke 1981, RCC 1992), and it is close to formal concept analysis. The link between his 'géométrie modérée' programme and mereotopology is not made in the literature.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historians and logicians studying point-free foundations of tame geometry would find a Grothendieck-authored axiomatic attempt in this direction. It is minor mathematically but relevant to the reception of the Esquisse's tame-topology programme.

deep.surprise_reason: The computations are elementary verifications in a one-dimensional combinatorial model. The only notable point is historical: Grothendieck pursued tame topology through a polarity/mereotopological axiomatics, which is unpublished but not mathematically deep at this stage.
transcription_corrections: Header line reads 'Supp = Supp°({P_a})', meaning the closed and open supports coincide for a point; '92' is Grothendieck's page number and '101' at the bottom left is the archive foliation.
In Cor 3 the inserted 'Omb°(S_ab) =' sits above the right-hand side, so the intended reading is Supp°{S_ab} = Omb°(S_ab) = Supp({S_ab}) ∖ ∂S_ab, with ∂S_ab = {P_a, P_b} written beneath.
In Cor 1's proof the relation is written 'X |o| Y' (open foreignness), not '|·|'.
